title: Boundless consciousness
hookLine: what knows all that space? the second formless state turns to the knowing itself, and a Daoist neighbor widens into stillness too
tomorrow: what does a room look like right after everyone's left?

lines: FROM THE SPACE TO THE KNOWING.
cards: Music can fill a room so completely that nobody notices the listening. Then somebody asks: wait, who's hearing this? That's the turn the Visuddhimagga makes next.
Resting in boundless space, the meditator sees that space still sits close to form. So attention turns from the space to what was knowing the space. Consciousness, consciousness.

teach.b: So, the question for today: what is that knowing? The manual doesn't call it a soul or a hidden self. In Buddhist teaching, consciousness is one of the five aggregates, arising and passing with its conditions.

This state is wide and still, and it's still a state: it was made, so it ends. In one sutta the Buddha calls these formless states peaceful abidings, a good place to rest, and keeps them apart from the work that frees.
Now a neighbor. The Tao Te Ching, the Daoist classic of the Way, has its own picture of widening into stillness.

teach.h: ALL THINGS RISE, AND GO BACK.
teach.b: Chapter sixteen, in plain words: empty yourself all the way, hold fast to stillness; all things rise, and I watch them go back. Going back to the root is stillness.
Shared ground: both teach widening into quiet, and watching things rise and settle without grabbing at them.
One honest difference: for the Tao Te Ching, stillness is a return to the root, the Way that all things come from.
For the Visuddhimagga, boundless consciousness is a place the mind passes through, not a source it returns to.

how: The base of boundless consciousness is the second of four formless attainments in Theravada meditation manuals, practiced after the base of boundless space by meditators with deep concentration.

o: knowing what other people are thinking
resting in the wide awareness that knows space
a hidden soul that never changes or dies

games.q: the knowing, and a neighbor — tap the pairs.
p: the Buddha's name for formless states
going back to the root is stillness

s: boundless consciousness is the Buddhist name for a permanent soul
in Buddhist teaching consciousness arises and passes with conditions; this is a peaceful state, and still a state.
the Tao Te Ching's chapter sixteen speaks of stillness and going back to the root
all things rise, and go back; going back to the root is stillness.
in one sutta the Buddha calls the formless states peaceful abidings
a good place to rest, kept apart from the work that frees.

games.q: a friend says meditation showed her a vast, still awareness, so it must be her permanent true self. what does the Visuddhimagga's teaching say?
o: yes: boundless awareness is the unchanging self the path is after.
it's peaceful, but still a state: it arose, so it passes.
she imagined it; awareness can't feel wide at all.
games.why: in Buddhist teaching consciousness is one of the aggregates, arising with conditions. the manual honors the state and still treats it as a place the mind passes through.

practice: Close your eyes and notice sounds, sensations and thoughts, each one rising and fading. Then turn, gently, from what's known to the knowing itself, wide and without an edge you can find.
When something grabs you, notice that it's known, and widen again.

wordCard.voice: Boundless consciousness: the second formless state. Attention turns from boundless space to the awareness that knew it. Peaceful, and still a state.

orig.note: Pali: vinnana, consciousness, with ancayatana, the base of endlessness: the base of boundless consciousness.

carryVoice: For the road: boundless awareness, wide enough to hold a hard week. Thirty-four of forty, known.

sources.ref: Visuddhimagga 10 (the base consisting of boundless consciousness: seeing the base of boundless space as near to materiality, the meditator attends to the consciousness that pervaded the space as 'consciousness, consciousness')
Majjhima Nikaya 8 (Sallekha Sutta: the formless attainments are called peaceful abidings, not effacement)
Majjhima Nikaya 38 (consciousness arises dependent on conditions)
Tao Te Ching 16 (attain utmost emptiness, hold to stillness; all things arise and return; returning to the root is stillness)
